analysis.title: JPM US Market Intell Morning Briefing, November 12, 2026
key_insights: Premarket moves on Nov 12: SPX -0.3%, NDX -0.6%, RTY -0.0%. WTI -81bps at $85.83, gold -92bps at $3,951, 10Y at 4.994%, VIX at 18.23. Futures are lower after Wednesday's rally, which followed stronger CRWV earnings and a resumption of the AI trade.

NVDA is -5.8% premarket on CEO risk and the rest of the Mag7 are lower. Semis, software and memory are weaker, which the desk reads as profit-taking rather than a reversal. Semis have retraced all of their losses since the midterm election.
Ex-AI names have a bid, with healthcare and staples outperforming. The yield curve is flattening. Today's US macro focus is the 30Y bond auction and Fedspeak.
Europe is higher: DAX +1.1%, SX5E +0.4%, SXXP +0.4%, UKX +0.3%. Value and size lead, momentum and residual vol lag. Asia was lower: HSI -1.3%, CSI -0.8%, NKY -0.7%, KOSPI -0.6%.

Narrative: the AI trade resumption coincides with a higher-for-longer rates view after a material repricing higher following Tuesday's CPI print. The desk does not treat the two as mutually exclusive but is hesitant to declare an all clear for AI/Tech because selling volumes are rising on up-days in Tech and Semis. It sees broader markets higher.

If the yield curve keeps flattening, the desk sees a rotation from cyclicals toward value, which argues for Europe over US counterparts. Hyperscalers could become the main beneficiary of residual weakness in semis and AI.

Manish Sinha: rotation risk in semiconductors (SMH) is increasing, with the possibility of a 10% pullback. Wednesday's move came on light liquidity. AI Momentum (JPAIMOPR) opened up 50 bps and closed down 1%, so investors have not yet chased the rally. CoreWeave sits on the laggard side of AI Momentum and NVIDIA on the leader side.

Positioning Intelligence: a week after the midterms, clients on JPM's books are closing gaps and neutralizing risk, mostly by covering shorts, rather than chasing moves. There is room to add risk, but conviction has yet to rebuild.

Global equity futures positioning rose from -0.9z to -0.1z (45th percentile over 12 months). US aggregate rates positioning rose from -1.4z (11th percentile) a month ago to +0.5z (75th percentile). Short exposure fell about 2z over the month while long exposure rose about 0.5z.
The NDX vs RTY positioning gap, at the 96th percentile on Oct 7, has closed sharply. Positioning now only modestly favors NDX because RTY positioning is still light.

Rates positioning: Tuesday yields rose across the curve, led by the front end (2Y +0.18%, 10Y +0.11%). Clients bought the 2Y into the selloff (+1.9z one day) and trimmed the long end (T-Bond -1.7z). Gilt positioning is -1.6z (6th percentile since 2020) as shorts were added. JGB positioning is at a 12-month high (+2.3z).

Equity positioning: Stoxx 50 is at a 12-month high (+2.9z, 98th percentile since 2020), up from +1.9z, driven by short covering, with short exposure the lowest in a year. UK is near its lows (-1.6z). Korea was bought into the drawdown (+1.7z over the week) while KOSPI fell 7% on the week.

Commodity positioning: WTI positioning fell from +0.9z to +0.3z (41st percentile) as crude fell about 11% over the week. US nat gas positioning moved from -2.9z to -2.6z on short covering with prices +14%.

Nikos: weekly equity fund flows show retail remains bullish and keeps buying the dip in November after strong October buying. Retail call-option buying has retrenched from its early-June peak, leaving room for the retail impulse to build. Equity momentum reversal and the collapse of AI-stock P/E multiples point to an extreme reversal of the AI trade.
Oracle CDS trading volumes have subsided since their peak in the week ending Oct 23, possibly signaling calmer neocloud funding fears.

US Market Intel view: Nov 10's CPI-driven move is an opportunity to reset bond yields higher to match growth. Q3 2026 GDP printed about 3.4%, the economy is on track for above-trend growth into 2027, and earnings season was robust. The desk is Tactically Bullish.

Monetization Menu: the Tech washout appears at or near completion, though another semis decline is possible. The desk likes broad Tech and would consider US memory and semis via options. CRWV, OpenAI Q3 revenue and capital-markets reopening support the AI theme, but moves may stay choppy as yields shift higher. Cyclicals are better played through European names over US ones given lower positioning and valuation.

The recession basket (JPRECES) is +14.9% since Sep 30 while SPX -1.7%, NDX -8.8%, SOXX -22.7% and DRAM -32.7%. The desk argues a drop in AI capex is unlikely to cause a recession because it added little to jobs, the wealth effect is second order, AI capex offsets via more negative net exports, and consumers hold large cash balances in a full-employment labor market. Financing risks exist but are unlikely to be as systemic as before the GFC.

Mike Feroli (JPM): nonresidential construction, contractor and heavy/civil engineering jobs rose 165,000 over the year, only 0.1% of total employment. This may explain the backlash against data centers, and a policy-related pullback in data-center spending should have limited job-growth impact. Professional, scientific and technical services jobs rose 33,000, a glimmer that AI job loss is far off, though one month proves little.

Dubravko Lakos-Bujas reiterates a YE26 SPX target of 8,000 on $365 EPS at 21.9x, implying 8.4% upside from Friday's close. Economics expects trend-like US growth in 2027 with modest disinflation, and his team estimates EPS growth of about 20%.

Dubravko on the unwind: it is a de-leveraging event. Investors held record leverage in AI plays, liquidity dissipated from late June, and systematic and vol strategies plus buyside liquidations magnified it. October was the largest single-month Long Momentum unwind, about -11% or 6 standard deviations, with Momentum L/S down about 40% from its peak.

Equity multiples have compressed about 4x since January, one of the most extreme de-ratings outside recessions, while earnings grew double digits. Since May, AI multiples compressed about 35%: semis 52%, hyperscalers 14%, memory 60%, processing units 50%.

Dubravko sees the selling as far along: Momentum crowding reset from the 100th to the 76th percentile, levered ETF sales of about $60bn Thursday and $35bn the prior Friday took exposure below Jan 2026 levels, CTAs flipped net short with perhaps $50bn left to sell, dealer net gamma imbalance sits at the 12th percentile, $1.2T of announced buybacks should support, and QQQ RSI below 30 has on average preceded a roughly 4% rally over five days.

Dubravko's catalysts: Middle East developments, megacap IPOs, next month's ERCOT meeting (AI capex implications) and the December Fed meeting. He sees the midterms as a clearing event and data-center headwinds as less onerous than priced.

Dubravko estimates each $100B of AI capex adds about $9 to 2027 S&P 500 EPS (about 2.5% growth). Capex at the middle of the range, about $1.5T, would add roughly $18 vs consensus, or 4-5% to 2027 EPS growth. JPM credit analysts expect hyperscalers to fund 2027 capex absent credit shocks, but the funding mix needs more equity.

News links flag: Goolsbee called the inflation report 'borderline disturbing' as the Fed weighs more hikes, a Reuters piece on a possible 50 bps hike under Warsh's Fed, CoreWeave's CEO canceling a planned share sale, and Nvidia scrutiny of Jensen Huang ahead of earnings.
